claim: Naïve human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) share transcriptional and epigenomic signatures with trophoblast cells.
source: As naïve hPSCs share transcriptional and epigenomic signatures with trophoblast cells, it has been proposed that the naïve state may have enhanced predisposition for differentiation along this extraembryonic lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work and is stated in the abstract as background information.

claim: Naïve hPSCs can directly give rise to human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs).
source: We found that naïve hPSCs can directly give rise to human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs) and undergo further differentiation into both extravillous and syncytiotrophoblast.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Naïve hPSCs can undergo further differentiation into both extravillous and syncytiotrophoblast.
source: We found that naïve hPSCs can directly give rise to human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs) and undergo further differentiation into both extravillous and syncytiotrophoblast.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing differentiation into EVT and STB.

claim: Primed hPSCs do not support hTSC derivation.
source: In contrast, primed hPSCs do not support hTSC derivation, but give rise to non-self-renewing cytotrophoblasts in response to BMP4.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing naïve and primed hPSCs.

claim: Primed hPSCs give rise to non-self-renewing cytotrophoblasts in response to BMP4.
source: In contrast, primed hPSCs do not support hTSC derivation, but give rise to non-self-renewing cytotrophoblasts in response to BMP4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on BMP4-directed differentiation.

claim: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are similar to blastocyst-derived hTSCs.
source: Global transcriptome and chromatin accessibility analyses indicate that hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are similar to blastocyst-derived hTSCs and acquire features of post-implantation trophectoderm.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data comparing naïve-derived and blastocyst-derived hTSCs.

claim: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs acquire features of post-implantation trophectoderm.
source: Global transcriptome and chromatin accessibility analyses indicate that hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are similar to blastocyst-derived hTSCs and acquire features of post-implantation trophectoderm.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis comparing naïve hTSCs to embryonic trophectoderm at different developmental stages.

claim: The naïve pluripotent epiblast compartment within the inner cell mass (ICM) of the blastocyst constitutes a naïve or ground state of pluripotency.
source: Prior to implantation, the pluripotent epiblast compartment within the inner cell mass (ICM) of the blastocyst constitutes a naïve or ground state of pluripotency (Nakamura et al., 2016; Nichols and Smith, 2009; Stirparo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The naïve state can be captured in vitro in the form of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
source: This naïve state can be captured in vitro in the form of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: After implantation, transcription factors associated with naïve pluripotency are downregulated and pluripotent cells become primed for differentiation.
source: After implantation, transcription factors associated with naïve pluripotency are downregulated and pluripotent cells become primed for differentiation in response to signals from the surrounding extraembryonic tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about developmental progression.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) derived under conventional conditions represent a primed pluripotent state.
source: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) derived under conventional conditions are thought to represent a primed pluripotent state, and were shown to correspond transcriptionally to the late post-implantation epiblast in a non-human primate model (Nakamura et al., 2016; Nichols and Smith, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Conventional hESCs correspond transcriptionally to the late post-implantation epiblast in a non-human primate model.
source: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) derived under conventional conditions are thought to represent a primed pluripotent state, and were shown to correspond transcriptionally to the late post-implantation epiblast in a non-human primate model (Nakamura et al., 2016; Nichols and Smith, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two transgene-free culture systems, 5i/L/A and t2i/L/Gö, induce defining transcriptional and epigenetic features of the human pre-implantation epiblast.
source: In particular, two transgene-free culture systems, 5i/L/A and t2i/L/Gö, were shown to induce defining transcriptional and epigenetic features of the human pre-implantation epiblast (Huang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Stirparo et al., 2018; Takashima et al., 2014; Theunissen et al., 2016; Theunissen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Naïve hESCs have offered insights into the mechanisms governing X-linked dosage compensation.
source: For example, naïve hESCs have offered insights into the mechanisms governing X-linked dosage compensation (Sahakyan et al., 2017), the role of human-specific transposable elements that are expressed in the pre-implantation embryo (Pontis et al., 2019; Theunissen et al., 2016), and the mechanisms leading to activation of naïve-specific enhancers (Pastor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hESCs are unresponsive to direct application of embryonic inductive cues.
source: While naïve hESCs are unresponsive to direct application of embryonic inductive cues, they acquire the capacity to undergo efficient multi-lineage differentiation upon treatment with a Wnt inhibitor, a process called 'capacitation' (Rostovskaya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hESCs acquire the capacity to undergo efficient multi-lineage differentiation upon treatment with a Wnt inhibitor, a process called 'capacitation'.
source: While naïve hESCs are unresponsive to direct application of embryonic inductive cues, they acquire the capacity to undergo efficient multi-lineage differentiation upon treatment with a Wnt inhibitor, a process called 'capacitation' (Rostovskaya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gene expression studies revealed a pronounced upregulation in naïve relative to primed hESCs of trophoblast-associated transcription factors, including ELF3, GCM1, and TFAP2C.
source: Gene expression studies revealed a pronounced upregulation in naïve relative to primed hESCs of trophoblast-associated transcription factors, including ELF3, GCM1, and TFAP2C (Theunissen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chromatin accessibility studies indicated that naïve hESCs share a broad panel of open chromatin sites with first-trimester placental tissues.
source: In addition, chromatin accessibility studies indicated that naïve hESCs share a broad panel of open chromatin sites with first-trimester placental tissues (Pontis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Embryonic and extraembryonic lineage markers are briefly co-expressed in the late morula and early blastocyst according to single cell RNA-seq studies of human pre-implantation embryos.
source: Intriguingly, embryonic and extraembryonic lineage markers are briefly co-expressed in the late morula and early blastocyst according to single cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) studies of human pre-implantation embryos (Petropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hESCs exhibit significantly enriched expression of trophoblast markers ELF5, KRT7, TFAP2C, GATA3, TEAD4, and CDX2 in embryoid bodies compared to primed hESCs.
source: Significantly enriched expression of trophoblast markers was observed in EBs derived from naïve compared to primed hESCs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Many trophoblast markers were already elevated in naïve versus primed hESCs prior to EB formation.
source: Furthermore, many of the examined trophoblast markers were already elevated in naïve versus primed hESCs prior to EB formation (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), consistent with our prior transcriptome analysis (Theunissen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data and citation to prior transcriptome analysis.

claim: Naïve hESCs treated with BMP4 do not survive.
source: However, when naïve hESCs were subjected to a protocol for BMP4-directed differentiation into cytotrophoblast (CTB) progenitors (Horii et al., 2016), the cells did not survive (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Naïve hESCs treated with StemPro for five passages re-gain competence for BMP4-directed trophoblast differentiation.
source: Indeed, naïve hESCs treated with StemPro for five passages re-gained competence for BMP4-directed trophoblast differentiation, as shown by the expression of several CTB markers (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Capacitated naïve hESCs undergo BMP4-directed trophoblast differentiation more efficiently than primed hESCs.
source: Capacitated cells could not only readily undergo Step I CTB differentiation, but did so more efficiently than primed hESCs based on analysis of trophoblast-specific transcripts and proteins (Figure 1F,G; Figure 1—figure supplements 1D and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Naïve hPSCs acquired a typical hTSC-like morphology within several passages when cultured in hTSC media.
source: Naïve hPSCs acquired a typical hTSC-like morphology within several passages and could be expanded for at least 20 passages while maintaining a high proliferation rate (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Naïve hPSCs could be expanded for at least 20 passages in hTSC media while maintaining a high proliferation rate.
source: Naïve hPSCs acquired a typical hTSC-like morphology within several passages and could be expanded for at least 20 passages while maintaining a high proliferation rate (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Primed hPSCs did not acquire an hTSC-like morphology, even after prolonged culture in hTSC media.
source: In contrast, the parental primed hPSCs did not acquire an hTSC-like morphology, even after prolonged culture in hTSC media (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Naïve hTSCs uniformly express ITGA6 and EGFR.
source: We found that naïve hTSCs uniformly express ITGA6 and EGFR, two commonly used cell surface markers that mark both CTBs and hTSCs (Bischof and Irminger-Finger, 2005; Horii et al., 2016; Okae et al., 2018), in contrast to primed hPSCs that had been expanded in hTSC media (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Naïve hTSCs expressed significantly higher levels of ELF5, KRT7, GATA3, TFAP2C, and TEAD4 transcripts compared to primed hPSCs cultured in hTSC media.
source: The naïve hTSCs also expressed significantly higher levels of ELF5, KRT7, GATA3, TFAP2C, and TEAD4 transcripts (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Naïve hTSCs exhibited almost no CDX2 expression, which is consistent with hTSCs derived from blastocysts or first-trimester placental tissues.
source: Notably, naïve hTSCs exhibited almost no CDX2 expression, which is consistent with hTSCs derived from blastocysts or first-trimester placental tissues (Okae et al., 2018; Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data and citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hTSCs expressed the hTSC markers KRT7, TEAD4, and TP63 at the protein level.
source: Naïve hTSCs also expressed the hTSC markers KRT7, TEAD4, and TP63 at the protein level (Lee et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013; Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis for CD75 and SUSD2 confirmed the loss of naïve identity in naïve hTSCs.
source: Flow cytometry analysis for CD75 and SUSD2, two naïve-specific cell surface markers (Bredenkamp et al., 2019a; Collier et al., 2017), confirmed the loss of naïve identity in naïve hTSCs (Figure 2F), which was further corroborated by downregulation of KLF17 transcript (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Primed hPSCs did not upregulate trophoblast markers when cultured in hTSC media, but instead exhibited increased expression of VIM and PAX6.
source: Conversely, primed hPSCs did not upregulate trophoblast markers when cultured in hTSC media, but instead exhibited increased expression of VIM and PAX6, suggesting the acquisition of a neuroectodermal fate (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Naïve hTSCs derived from PXGL-cultured naïve hPSCs closely resemble those derived from 5i/L/A-cultured naïve hPSCs.
source: Both morphological and molecular analyses indicated that naïve hTSCs derived from PXGL-cultured naïve hPSCs closely resemble those derived from 5i/L/A-cultured naïve hPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is supported by morphological and molecular data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: Naïve hTSC-derivation is an intrinsic property of the naïve state of human pluripotency, regardless of the specific culture condition used.
source: This suggests that naïve hTSC-derivation is likely an intrinsic property of the naïve state of human pluripotency, regardless of the specific culture condition used.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that naïve hTSCs can be derived from naïve hPSCs cultured in different media.

claim: Naïve hPSCs can give rise to naïve hTSCs on a clonal level.
source: Additionally, we investigated whether naïve hPSCs can give rise to naïve hTSCs on a clonal level, which would preclude that hTSCs arise from a small population of pre-existing trophoblast-like cells in the culture.
evidence: This is supported by clonal expansion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: About 90% of EVT-like cells derived from naïve hTSCs were positive for HLA-G.
source: Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that about 90% of EVT-like cells were positive for HLA-G (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression and secretion of MMP2 was detected in EVT-like cells derived from naïve hTSCs by ELISA and immunofluorescence staining.
source: Similarly, expression and secretion of MMP2 was detected by ELISA and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EVT-like cells derived from naïve hTSCs have invasive potential, in contrast to the naïve hTSCs from which they were derived.
source: The results indicate that our EVT-like cells have invasive potential, in contrast to the naïve hTSCs from which they were derived (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Naïve hTSC-derived 3D STB-like cells exhibited a cyst-like morphology typical for 3D STBs.
source: The naïve hTSC-derived 3D STB-like cells exhibited a cyst-like morphology typical for 3D STBs (Okae et al., 2018; Figure 3H), and expressed the STB markers hCG and SDC1 based on immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR analysis (Jokimaa et al., 1998; Strumpf et al., 2005; Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations and molecular data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Naïve hTSC-derived 3D STB-like cells expressed the STB markers hCG and SDC1.
source: The naïve hTSC-derived 3D STB-like cells exhibited a cyst-like morphology typical for 3D STBs (Okae et al., 2018; Figure 3H), and expressed the STB markers hCG and SDC1 based on immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR analysis (Jokimaa et al., 1998; Strumpf et al., 2005; Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I–K.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis confirmed downregulation of the hTSC-specific marker TEAD4 in STB-like cells.
source: Finally, qRT-PCR analysis confirmed downregulation of the hTSC-specific marker TEAD4 (Figure 3L), indicating the loss of hTSC identity.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are capable of undergoing further differentiation into two specialized trophoblast cell types, EVT and STB.
source: These morphological and molecular data demonstrate that hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are capable, at least at the population level, of undergoing further differentiation into two specialized trophoblast cell types, EVT and STB.
evidence: This is supported by the differentiation experiments and molecular characterization.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed that RNA-seq samples clustered together based on cell type, rather than genetic background.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the samples clustered together based on cell type, rather than genetic background (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pluripotent and trophoblast identities were predominantly divided along principal component 1 (PC1), which accounted for 41% of the variation in gene expression.
source: Pluripotent and trophoblast identities were predominantly divided along principal component 1 (PC1), which accounted for 41% of the variation in gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Naïve hTSCs and BT5 hTSCs clustered together very closely on the PCA plot.
source: It is worth noting that naïve hTSCs and BT5 hTSCs clustered together very closely on the PCA plot (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Naïve hTSCs express key trophoblast marker genes at comparable or even higher levels than the bona fide, BT5 hTSCs.
source: Further examination indicated that naïve hTSCs express key trophoblast marker genes at comparable or even higher levels than the bona fide, BT5 hTSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Naïve hTSCs displayed strong upregulation of many transcripts associated with trophoblast development.
source: Naïve hTSCs displayed strong upregulation of many transcripts associated with trophoblast development, whereas primed cells instead acquired neuroectodermal characteristics in hTSC media (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Primed hPSCs acquired neuroectodermal characteristics when cultured in hTSC media.
source: Naïve hTSCs displayed strong upregulation of many transcripts associated with trophoblast development, whereas primed cells instead acquired neuroectodermal characteristics in hTSC media (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: hTSCs cluster the most closely amongst themselves, as well as with day 10 and day 12 TE.
source: We found that hTSCs cluster the most closely amongst themselves, as well as with day 10 and day 12 TE (Figure 4E), while showing the best correlation with day 12 TE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: hTSCs show the best correlation with day 12 TE.
source: We found that hTSCs cluster the most closely amongst themselves, as well as with day 10 and day 12 TE (Figure 4E), while showing the best correlation with day 12 TE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: hTSCs correlate poorly with the EPI or PE lineages.
source: In contrast, the hTSCs correlate poorly with the EPI or PE lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are comparable to bona fide, blastocyst-derived hTSCs.
source: We conclude that hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are comparable to bona fide, blastocyst-derived hTSCs, and are transcriptionally the most similar to human post-implantation TE at day 12.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis comparing naïve-derived and blastocyst-derived hTSCs.

claim: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are transcriptionally the most similar to human post-implantation TE at day 12.
source: We conclude that hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs are comparable to bona fide, blastocyst-derived hTSCs, and are transcriptionally the most similar to human post-implantation TE at day 12.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis comparing naïve hTSCs to embryonic trophectoderm at different developmental stages.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks in all three hTSC lines are highly correlated globally.
source: Overall, we found ATAC-seq peaks in all three hTSC lines to be highly correlated globally (Figure 4F), which indicates that derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs induces a similar epigenomic profile as hTSC derivation from the human blastocyst.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs induces a similar epigenomic profile as hTSC derivation from the human blastocyst.
source: Overall, we found ATAC-seq peaks in all three hTSC lines to be highly correlated globally (Figure 4F), which indicates that derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs induces a similar epigenomic profile as hTSC derivation from the human blastocyst.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Naïve hESC-specific open chromatin sites are more enriched over promoter regions and tend to be in closer proximity to the nearest transcriptional start site relative to hTSC-specific open chromatin sites.
source: We identified differentially accessible regions (DARs) between naïve hESCs (9,059) and naïve hTSCs (12,132), and found that naïve hESC-specific open chromatin sites are more enriched over promoter regions (1,084) and tend to be in closer proximity to the nearest transcriptional start site relative to hTSC-specific open chromatin sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: A higher percentage of hTSC-specific DARs are located in intronic and intergenic regions.
source: In hTSCs, only 208 DARs are located in gene promoter regions, and a higher percentage of hTSC-specific DARs are located in intronic and intergenic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B), suggesting the importance of distal regulatory elements during differentiation of naïve hPSCs into hTSCs.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The importance of distal regulatory elements during differentiation of naïve hPSCs into hTSCs is suggested by the distribution of hTSC-specific DARs.
source: In hTSCs, only 208 DARs are located in gene promoter regions, and a higher percentage of hTSC-specific DARs are located in intronic and intergenic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B), suggesting the importance of distal regulatory elements during differentiation of naïve hPSCs into hTSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of DARs.

claim: The promoter regions of hTSC-specific genes are already accessible in naïve hESCs.
source: However, the ATAC-seq signal at the promoter regions of cluster 3 (hTSC-specific) genes was only slightly increased in naïve hTSCs relative to naïve hESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C). This indicates that the promoter regions of hTSC-specific genes are already accessible in naïve hESCs, which is consistent with previous findings that naïve hPSCs share open chromatin regions with first-trimester placental tissues (Pontis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hESC-specific enrichment was observed for the POU5F1:SOX2 and KLF4 motifs.
source: Naïve hESC-specific enrichment was observed for the POU5F1:SOX2 and KLF4 motifs (Figure 4G), consistent with the roles of these transcription factors in regulating naïve pluripotency (Guo et al., 2009; Stuart et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Significant enrichment for motifs associated with TEAD4, CEBP, GATA, and TFAP2 was observed over non-promoter regions in naïve hTSCs.
source: Intriguingly, we observed significant enrichment for motifs associated with TEAD4, CEBP, GATA, and TFAP2 over non-promoter regions in naïve hTSCs, while motifs associated with TFAP2, GATA, SP1, ELK1, and GRHL were enriched over promoter regions in naïve hTSCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Motifs associated with TFAP2, GATA, SP1, ELK1, and GRHL were enriched over promoter regions in naïve hTSCs.
source: Intriguingly, we observed significant enrichment for motifs associated with TEAD4, CEBP, GATA, and TFAP2 over non-promoter regions in naïve hTSCs, while motifs associated with TFAP2, GATA, SP1, ELK1, and GRHL were enriched over promoter regions in naïve hTSCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: TEAD4 and TFAP2 are known to be expressed in human TE.
source: Among these transcription factors, TEAD4 and TFAP2 are known to be expressed in human TE (Petropoulos et al., 2016), while CEBP and GATA factors have been implicated as regulators of trophoblast-specific HLA-G expression at the maternal-fetal interface (Ferreira et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CEBP and GATA factors have been implicated as regulators of trophoblast-specific HLA-G expression at the maternal-fetal interface.
source: Among these transcription factors, TEAD4 and TFAP2 are known to be expressed in human TE (Petropoulos et al., 2016), while CEBP and GATA factors have been implicated as regulators of trophoblast-specific HLA-G expression at the maternal-fetal interface (Ferreira et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Verteporfin treatment induced widespread cell death within several days when applied during hTSC derivation.
source: Verteporfin treatment induced widespread cell death within several days when applied during hTSC derivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Verteporfin had a detrimental effect on viability when applied to naïve hPSCs.
source: We then tested the effect of Verteporfin on the maintenance of naïve hPSCs and found that it had a similar detrimental effect on viability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: YAP is nuclear in both the TE and EPI in human blastocysts.
source: Unlike in the mouse embryo, where YAP is nuclear in the TE and cytoplasmic in the EPI compartment (Nishioka et al., 2009), YAP is nuclear in both the TE and EPI in human blastocysts (Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: YAP shows nuclear localization in both naïve hPSCs and hTSCs.
source: We confirmed by immunofluorescence analysis that YAP shows nuclear localization in both naïve hPSCs and hTSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: YAP-TEAD4 may contribute to both EPI and TE development in human.
source: Thus, YAP-TEAD4 may contribute to both EPI and TE development in human, potentially by targeting different regulatory elements and transcription factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the nuclear localization of YAP in both cell types.

claim: Naïve hPSCs have enhanced potential to access trophoblast fates during both spontaneous differentiation assays and upon treatment with conditions for hTSC isolation.
source: Our data now provide functional evidence that naïve hPSCs indeed have enhanced potential to access trophoblast fates during both spontaneous differentiation assays and upon treatment with recently devised conditions for hTSC isolation (Okae et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Primed hPSCs give rise to cells with a neuroectodermal gene expression profile when exposed to hTSC media.
source: While naïve hPSCs can directly give rise to bipotent hTSCs, primed hPSCs instead give rise to cells with a neuroectodermal gene expression profile when exposed to the same signaling milieu.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis.

claim: The enhanced, transgene-independent extraembryonic potential of naïve hPSCs is a distinctive functional attribute of naïve human pluripotency.
source: We propose that the enhanced, transgene-independent extraembryonic potential of naïve hPSCs is a distinctive functional attribute of naïve human pluripotency, which may reflect the co-expression of embryonic and extraembryonic genes in the human pre-implantation embryo (Petropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve, but not primed, hPSCs can give rise to human extraembryonic endoderm (XEN) cells in response to XEN media.
source: This conclusion is further corroborated by recent work demonstrating that naïve, but not primed, hPSCs can give rise to human extraembryonic endoderm (XEN) cells in response to XEN media (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: hTSC-like cells have been obtained from human expanded potential stem cells (hEPSCs).
source: The capacity to attain an hTSC-like state does not, however, appear to be restricted to the naïve state. hTSC-like cells have also been obtained from human expanded potential stem cells (hEPSCs) (Gao et al., 2019), while another study reported that putative hTSCs can be derived from primed hPSCs after transition into a CTB-like state (Mischler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Putative hTSCs can be derived from primed hPSCs after transition into a CTB-like state.
source: The capacity to attain an hTSC-like state does not, however, appear to be restricted to the naïve state. hTSC-like cells have also been obtained from human expanded potential stem cells (hEPSCs) (Gao et al., 2019), while another study reported that putative hTSCs can be derived from primed hPSCs after transition into a CTB-like state (Mischler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Primed hPSCs are most closely aligned with the late post-implantation epiblast based on scRNA-seq studies.
source: However, primed hPSCs are most closely aligned with the late post-implantation epiblast based on scRNA-seq studies (Nakamura et al., 2016), when TE and EPI lineages have already segregated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Primed hPSCs have substantially elevated levels of DNA methylation compared to pre-implantation embryos, naïve hPSCs, or hTSCs.
source: Primed hPSCs also have substantially elevated levels of DNA methylation compared to pre-implantation embryos, naïve hPSCs, or hTSCs (Okae et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2014; Theunissen et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Putative CTB progenitors derived from primed hPSCs upon BMP4 treatment may actually correspond to an extraembryonic mesoderm identity.
source: Hence, it has been proposed that putative CTB progenitors derived from primed hPSCs upon BMP4 treatment may actually correspond to an extraembryonic mesoderm identity (Bernardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BMP4 treatment alone induces a mixture of trophoblast and mesoderm fates in primed hPSCs.
source: Recent work from the Parast lab confirms that BMP4 treatment alone induces a mixture of trophoblast and mesoderm fates in primed hPSCs (Horii et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The BMP4-mediated differentiation protocol may be primed-state specific.
source: Our data indicate that naïve hPSCs are unresponsive to BMP4 (Figure 1C), in accordance with recent findings that naïve hPSCs are recalcitrant to direct application of some lineage-inductive cues (Rostovskaya et al., 2019), and may in fact suggest that the BMP4-mediated differentiation protocol is primed-state specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs presents a novel experimental paradigm to identify early determinants of human trophoblast specification.
source: We propose that the derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs presents a novel experimental paradigm to identify early determinants of human trophoblast specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: TEAD4 plays an important role in human TE development.
source: Intriguingly, the TEAD4 binding motif is significantly enriched at the open non-promoter regions specific to naïve and primary hTSCs. This suggests that TEAD4 plays an important role in human TE development.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The HIPPO/YAP signaling pathway is involved in mouse TE specification.
source: It may also indicate that the HIPPO/YAP signaling pathway, a known regulator of TEAD4 (Zhao et al., 2008), is involved in mouse as well as human TE specification (Nishioka et al., 2009; Nishioka et al., 2008; Yagi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TFAP2C, a trophoblast-specific transcription factor in mouse, plays an essential role in naïve human pluripotency.
source: This divergence is not unprecedented: TFAP2C, a trophoblast-specific transcription factor in mouse, was shown to play an essential role in naïve human pluripotency as well (Pastor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naïve hPSCs provide a scalable source of cellular material for hTSC derivation.
source: Thus far, the isolation of hTSCs has required the use of blastocysts or first-trimester placental tissues (Okae et al., 2018), neither of which are readily accessible or amenable to genetic manipulation. In contrast, naïve hPSCs can be conveniently derived from any pre-existing line of hPSCs and can undergo efficient genetic modification (Yang et al., 2016). Thus, naïve hPSCs provide a scalable source of cellular material for hTSC derivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of naïve hPSCs and supported by citations.

claim: Several groups have described protocols for direct reprogramming of human somatic cells into naïve pluripotency.
source: Furthermore, several groups have recently described protocols for direct reprogramming of human somatic cells into naïve pluripotency (Giulitti et al., 2019; Kilens et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The derivation of naïve iPSCs from patient-specific cells and their subsequent differentiation into hTSCs may provide a pathway to uncover the genetic origins of common pathologies afflicting the trophoblast lineage.
source: The derivation of naïve iPSCs from patient-specific cells and their subsequent differentiation into hTSCs may provide a pathway to uncover the genetic origins of common pathologies afflicting the trophoblast lineage, such as miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, and fetal growth restriction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.
